title: this in Methods
concept: When called as a method, this refers to the object that owns the method

steps.title: Create user Object
steps.explanation: Create a user object with a name property and a greet method.

steps.title: Call user.greet()
steps.explanation:
Call greet as a method of the user object.
The object before the dot (.) becomes this!
steps.keyInsight: When called as obj.method(), this = obj
steps.analogy: The object before the dot becomes the owner of the function.

steps.title: Access this.name
steps.explanation: Since this points to user, this.name is 'Alice'.

steps.title: Copy the Function Reference
steps.explanation:
Assign user.greet to the greetFn variable.
Only the function itself is copied — the connection to the object is severed!
steps.keyInsight: Storing a function in a variable breaks its connection to the object.

steps.title: Call greetFn() — this Lost!
steps.explanation:
greetFn() is a regular function call.
There's no object before the dot, so this is the global object (or undefined)!
steps.keyInsight: Storing a method in a variable and calling it loses this!
steps.misconception: It's easy to assume this is still user since greetFn was originally user.greet.

steps.title: Access this.name (this Lost)
steps.explanation:
Inside greetFn, we access `this.name`.
But this is window (or undefined), so `this.name` is **undefined**!
steps.keyInsight: The same code (line 4), but this is different, so the result is different.

quiz.explanation:
fn() is a regular function call.
this becomes the global object, and since there's no value on the global object, undefined is returned.

misconceptions.wrong: this is preserved even after assigning a method to a variable
misconceptions.correct:
It's not.
The moment you put `obj.method` into a variable, it loses its connection to `obj` and becomes a plain function.
misconceptions.why:
In JavaScript, functions are **not bound** to objects.
The object is only 'borrowed' temporarily when you call through the dot notation.

misconceptions.wrong: this refers to the object in which the function was defined
misconceptions.correct: this refers to the object that called the function (the object before the dot).
misconceptions.why: The same function can have a different this depending on how it's called.

keyTakeaway: obj.method() → this = obj, fn() → this = global (this lost)
